<reason>Both sides argued the actual motion well, but CON's mid-to-late game was sharper. CON's pressure questions forced PRO to clarify that employers could act on "good-faith judgment," and CON then caught this as an unacknowledged amendment to the motion's actual text ("objectively does not materially affect"), a live inconsistency PRO never resolved in its closing. CON's distinction between "auditing the decision-maker" (motive-based, as in existing discrimination law) versus "auditing the world" (proving actual downstream harm) sharpened why PRO's analogy to existing fuzzy standards was weaker than claimed, and the ex ante/ex post framing (enumerated categories protect before acting; a general material-effect standard only resolves after litigation) was a genuinely original throughline that PRO's Q2/closing rebuttal did not fully neutralize. PRO scored real points too — turning CON's own hard examples (adviser, foreman, hospital worker) into proof the standard resolves correctly, and exposing that CON's preference for "enumerated categories" is arguably a concession that stronger protection in some form is desirable — but PRO's closing mostly re-asserted its concrete-vs-speculative-harm framing rather than directly re-engaging CON's sharpest late points (the textual catch, the motive-vs-world distinction), leaving them live and unanswered at the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 catching PRO's answer to Q1 ("good-faith judgment... show the firing responded to a genuine effect") as inconsistent with the motion's literal "objectively does not materially affect" language, reused decisively in CON's closing as proof PRO's standard "shapeshifts under pressure."</best_rebuttal>
